deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (fol. 185): the far field of a magnet SN with centre A, magnetic moment m and axis SN, at a point P with AP = r. u is the angle NAP. The force on positive magnetic fluid at P is F = (m/r^3)·(3(n·e_r)e_r − n), where n is the unit vector along AN. Gauss states tan v = ½ tan u and |F| = (m/r^3)·sqrt(4cos²u + sin²u) = (m/r^3)·sqrt(3cos²u + 1) = (m/r^3)·sqrt(5/2 + 3/2·cos 2u). He then gives three ways of splitting F into two components.

I (end of fol. 185):
- 3m·cos u/r^3 along AP;
- m/r^3 parallel to NS (that is, along −n).
This is literally F = (m/r^3)(3 cos u·e_r − n).

II (this page):
- 2m·cos u/r^3 along AP;
- m·sin u/r^3 along the perpendicular e_⊥, the direction making angle u+90° with AN.
My fill-in: n = cos u·e_r − sin u·e_⊥, so F = (m/r^3)(3cos u·e_r − cos u·e_r + sin u·e_⊥) = (m/r^3)(2cos u·e_r + sin u·e_⊥). This gives tan v = sin u/(2cos u) = ½ tan u, as on fol. 185.

III (this page):
- 3m/(2r^3) along AP', where angle NAP = angle PAP' (so AP' makes angle 2u with AN);
- m/(2r^3) parallel to SN (along +n).
My check in Cartesian coordinates (x along AN):
- F·r^3/m = (2cos²u − sin²u, 3 sin u cos u) = (½ + (3/2)cos 2u, (3/2) sin 2u) = (3/2)(cos 2u, sin 2u) + (1/2)(1, 0).
- This is exactly decomposition III.
- By the law of cosines its magnitude is sqrt(9/4 + 1/4 + (3/2)cos 2u) = sqrt(5/2 + (3/2)cos 2u). This explains the last form of the intensity on fol. 185.
III is the neat geometric construction of the dipole field: reflect the axis direction in AP and combine 3:1.

SECOND PART (serves fol. 187, 'Ruhige Hinüberführung zu einem andern Gleichgewichtszustand'): bringing a damped magnetometer needle to a new equilibrium without residual oscillation.

Notation on fol. 187:
- T is the swing time (half period).
- λ is the half Briggsian logarithmic decrement per swing, i.e. the decrement per quadrant of phase.
- R is a quadrant (90°).
- P = 2Rt/T and Q = 2Rt'/T.
- log p = −λP and log q = +λQ (log = log10).

My reconstruction of the physics: write the deviation from the current equilibrium as a complex phase-plane variable, which evolves by multiplication with 10^{−λφ}·e^{iφ}.
- Phase 1 (duration t): the needle rests at 0 and the equilibrium is switched to 1, so its state is 1 − p·e^{iP} at time t.
- Phase 2 (duration t'): the equilibrium is switched back to 0, and the needle must arrive at rest at 1. Running backward from that final state gives q·e^{−iQ} at time t.
- Phase 3: the equilibrium is switched to 1 again and the needle stays at rest.
- Continuity at time t: 1 − p·e^{iP} = q·e^{−iQ}. This gives Gauss's p cos P + q cos Q = 1 and p sin P = q sin Q.

This page eliminates q and Q:
- q² = 1 − 2p cos P + p²;
- tan Q = p sin P/(1 − p cos P);
- substitute both into log q = λQ (Q in quadrants, i.e. Q = arctan(...)/R with arctan in degrees).
The result is one equation in the single unknown P, since p = 10^{−λP}:
  log(1 − 2p cos P + pp) / Arc.tg[p sin P/(1 − p cos P)] = (2λ)/R.
Gauss writes λ/R; see errors.

Numerical check against fol. 187 (2λ = 0.081, λ = 0.0405, T = 41.6 s):
- P = 0.73554 quadrants = 66.20°, log p = 9.97021−10, p = 0.93371.
- 1 − 2p cos P + p² = 1.11801, whose log is 0.04844 ≈ 2 log q = 0.04850.
- arctan(0.85426/0.62309) = 53.89° = 0.59878 quadrants = Q.
- The ratio is 0.04844/53.89° ≈ 0.000899 ≈ 2λ/90°.
- t = P·T/2 = 15.30 s and t' = Q·T/2 = 12.45 s, as recorded. The '38^P 25' and '31^P 12' are the same times in 0.4-s beats.

The whole is a two-switch ('bang-off-bang') schedule that kills residual oscillation of a damped oscillator. This is a 19th-century instance of what control engineering later called posicast / input shaping.
errors: Factor-2 slip on this page: with the definitions of fol. 187 (log p = −λP, log q = +λQ, λ = half decrement), the eliminated equation should read log(1 − 2p cos P + pp)/Arc.tg(...) = 2λ/R, not λ/R. Gauss's own numbers (P = 0.73554, Q = 0.59878, λ = 0.0405) satisfy the 2λ/R version (0.04844/53.89° ≈ 0.0009 = 0.081/90) and not λ/R. Alternatively, λ on this page silently denotes the full decrement. The numerical solution on fol. 187 is correct either way.

Implicit convention: 'parallel mit SN' in III means the direction from S to N (+axis), whereas in I 'parallel mit NS' is the opposite direction. Both are correct as stated, but the distinction is only in the letter order.
No other errors: decompositions II and III are exactly correct.

results.what: Far-field components of a magnetic dipole: radial 2m cos u/r^3, transverse m sin u/r^3, with tan v = ½ tan u
results.modern_name: Dipole field in polar components (Gauss's tangent law for the first/second principal positions)
results.usually_credited_to: Coulomb/Poisson/Biot for the dipole law; Gauss, Intensitas vis magneticae (1832/33), for the precise use in measurement

results.what: Decomposition III: dipole field = (3m/2r^3) along the reflection of the axis in AP + (m/2r^3) along the axis; magnitude sqrt(5/2 + 3/2 cos 2u)
results.modern_name: Geometric construction of the dipole field direction (double-angle form B ∝ 3/2 e_{2u} + 1/2 e_0)
results.usually_credited_to: folklore geometric construction; no specific attribution known

results.what: Two-switch schedule (force on at 0, off at t, on at t+t') that brings a damped oscillator (magnetometer needle) to a new equilibrium at rest; conditions p cos P + q cos Q = 1, p sin P = q sin Q, reduced to one transcendental equation in P and solved numerically
results.modern_name: Posicast / input-shaping (bang-bang) control of a damped second-order system
results.usually_credited_to: O.J.M. Smith (posicast, 1957); Singer & Seering (input shaping, 1990). In 19th-c. practice, Gauss–Weber 'Beruhigung' methods for magnetometers (1830s).

deep.surprise_reason: The dipole formulas are standard Gauss material from 1832–39. The quiet-transfer computation is a clean, exact zero-residual-vibration switching schedule for a damped oscillator, conceptually the posicast/input-shaping idea of the 1950s. However, Gauss and Weber are known to have devised practical needle-calming procedures for the Göttingen magnetometers, and this is an application within that known context rather than a general theory. So it is a notable unpublished detail, not a major priority claim.

checkable.asserts: x-component of decomposition III equals the dipole field x-component (result 0)
y-component of decomposition III equals the dipole field y-component (result 0)
decomposition II equals decomposition I, i.e. the dipole field 3(n·e_r)e_r − n (zero vector)
magnitude from III equals sqrt(4cos^2u + sin^2u) (result 0)
for real p, P: q^2 = |1 − p e^{iP}|^2 = 1 − 2p cos P + p^2 (result 0)
p sin P − q sin Q ≈ 0 for Gauss's solution
p cos P + q cos Q − 1 ≈ 0 for Gauss's solution
t ≈ 15.30 s and t' ≈ 12.45 s for T = 41.6 s, as recorded on fol. 187

transcription_corrections: Item II first line: the image shows '2m/r³ cos u' with a stray/cancelled stroke before the fraction; the reading 2m/r^3 · cos u is correct.
'mit Einer unbekannten Grösse' – 'Einer' is underlined in the manuscript (emphasis: one unknown).
Next page (fol. 187): 'Q = 2Rt/T' should be read Q = 2Rt'/T; the numbers t' = 12.45 s ↔ Q = 0.59878 confirm this.
Equation on this page: the manuscript indeed reads λ/R, but mathematically this should be 2λ/R given p = 10^{−λP}; this is a slip by Gauss, not a transcription error.
